articles.title: In Kyrgyzstan, persons with disabilities are collecting proof of physical barriers to hold the government accountable
articles.summary: Lived experience can reveal things that a conventional audit may miss.
articles.content:
This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Kyrgyzstan’s progress in creating an inclusive and accessible environment for people with disabilities remains limited after seven years of ratifying the United Nations (UN) Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019.

Despite a legal responsibility to undertake measures that would remove legal and physical barriers and help people with disabilities lead independent social and economic lives, the government has not prioritized this commitment at the level requested by the country’s disabled community.

In such circumstances, holding the government accountable requires proof of how much physical infrastructure remains inaccessible for the more than 218,000 people with disabilities in the country — about three percent of the population.

One of the organizations leading this effort in Kyrgyzstan is the public fund “Oasis”, which is documenting the level of physical inaccessibility in the capital, Bishkek, with the help of people with disabilities who are auditing objects through their real-life experiences. Global Voices conducted a written interview with Oasis to learn about this work, which is being carried out under the Digital Sparks project. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Oasis (O): Founded in 2003, Oasis is a Kyrgyz civil society organization working to build inclusive communities where everyone can participate and reach their full potential. We joined the project because we know that it is not possible to build an inclusive city without listening to the people navigating its barriers every day. In Bishkek, we saw accessibility discussed through policies and assumptions, while lived experiences remained largely invisible. We wanted to change that to make exclusion visible, measurable, and impossible to overlook with the help of data. Digital Sparks helped us build the Oasis Data Lab, bringing together citizen-generated data, digital mapping, storytelling, and advocacy. Our goal was not simply to create a map, but to build a bridge between lived experience and public decision-making, turning everyday barriers into evidence for change.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

O: The project grew from a practical problem: people with disabilities face barriers across Bishkek, but these barriers were not being systematically documented. Public transport, entrances, ramps, toilets, signage, and other parts of the urban environment can make everyday participation difficult. Yet without reliable and regularly updated data, these problems remain easy to overlook. Kyrgyzstan ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019, but there is still a gap between formal commitments and everyday accessibility. Previous assessments were limited and did not create a living public record that could be used to monitor progress. We therefore started from a simple principle: before accessibility can be improved, it has to be measured. And the people who experience these barriers every day should be directly involved in producing that evidence.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

O: Through Digital Sparks, we developed Oasis Data Lab into a more structured space for digital civic participation. We brought together more than 30 young people, including people with physical disabilities, blind and low-vision participants, deaf participants, social activists, and urban experts. We organized workshops on disability rights, inclusivity, digital advocacy, data collection, mapping, and storytelling. A major practical change was integrating UrbanEyes into our work. Through the application, participants can assess buildings using geolocation, photographs, questionnaires, and standardized accessibility indicators. The web platform then visualizes this information through an interactive map, filters, heat maps, and accessibility indices. Most importantly, the project moved us from collecting individual complaints toward creating structured, comparable civic data that can support advocacy, dialogue with authorities, and evidence-based urban planning.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

O: One of the biggest impacts has been the shift in how participants are positioned: not simply as beneficiaries, but as researchers, digital monitors, and civic actors. Participants have already assessed 350 buildings across Bishkek and transformed their observations into geo-referenced data for the city’s accessibility map. The results show the scale of the problem clearly: 60.3 percent of assessed buildings had a ramp-related barrier, either because there was no ramp or because the existing ramp was difficult or unsuitable to use. The project also allows participants to compare accessibility across districts and types of buildings, rather than relying only on individual complaints. Just as importantly, participants are learning to communicate findings through digital storytelling and advocacy. Their lived experience is becoming structured evidence that can be presented directly to decision-makers and used to argue for concrete improvements.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

O: The project changed our understanding of digital democracy. We previously saw digital tools mainly as instruments for research, communication, and advocacy. Digital Sparks helped us understand their deeper democratic potential: digital democracy can change not only how information is shared, but who gets to produce it, whose voices are visible, and who participates in decision-making. Participatory mapping showed that technology can shift evidence production closer to communities themselves. People can document the barriers they experience, make them visible, and use this evidence to demand change. We also learned that digital democracy must be accessible, safe, and rights-based. More importantly, we realized that as society becomes increasingly digital, traditional forms of participation alone are no longer enough. Digital democracy offers an opportunity to make civic participation more inclusive, responsive, and effective.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

O: Our most valuable lesson is that “Nothing About Us Without Us” should apply not only to policymaking, but also to the evidence on which policy is based. Lived experience can reveal things that a conventional audit may miss. A checklist may show that a building has a ramp, while a wheelchair user can show that the ramp is too steep, slippery, too narrow, lacks handrails, or still does not allow independent access. We also learned that data must remain dynamic. Accessibility cannot be measured once and considered solved; information needs to be updated and connected to advocacy. Finally, data alone does not create change. Its value comes from combining reliable evidence with storytelling, community leadership, public communication, and structured dialogue with institutions. That combination is what turns information into civic power.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

articles.personality_title: Kyrgyzstan’s disabled community uses digital tools to map accessibility barriers
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Kyrgyzstan ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019. However, many public places in the country remain hard to access for people with disabilities. About 218,000 people living there face obstacles like missing ramps or unsuitable public transport, but these problems were not well documented.

**What happened** – A group called Oasis, a civil society organization in Kyrgyzstan, started a project to collect detailed information about these barriers. They worked with people who have disabilities to visit and assess over 350 buildings in the capital, Bishkek. Using a digital app called UrbanEyes, participants took photos, shared their experiences, and created maps showing where accessibility problems exist.

**Impact** – This effort turned personal experiences into clear, organized data. For example, they found that about 60% of the buildings assessed had problems with ramps. The data helps show the government exactly where improvements are needed. It also changes how people with disabilities are seen—from just needing help to being active researchers and advocates for change.

**What's next step** – Oasis plans to keep updating this information and use it to talk with city officials. They want the data to guide real improvements in public spaces. The project also teaches participants digital skills and advocacy, helping them take part in decisions that affect their lives.

**One-sentence takeaway** – People with disabilities in Kyrgyzstan are using digital tools and their own experiences to map accessibility problems and push for better, more inclusive public spaces.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia overturns death sentence for man over Facebook comment, Sri Lanka says
articles.summary: Anojan Sivarasa's case sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, spurring diplomatic efforts to seek clemency.
articles.content:
Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court has set aside the death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan migrant worker over a comment he made on Facebook, Colombo's Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra said.

Anojan Sivarasa, 27, was sentenced to death in September after a Saudi appellate court convicted him of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over his comment.

The case sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, spurring diplomatic efforts to seek clemency.

Saudi Arabia's top court set aside the sentence on Wednesday, Hemachandra said in a post on Facebook, where he thanked the authorities and legal teams of both nations for their efforts.

In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.

During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Sivarasa to respond in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.

Although Sivarasa promptly deleted the comment and posted an apology video, a screenshot of it was brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.

It is not clear if there will be further legal proceedings or whether Sivarasa will remain in detention, and for how long. He was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of three million Saudi riyals ($0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court.

Faizer Mustafa, a Sri Lankan lawmaker who is involved in legal negotiations with Saudi Arabia regarding Sivarasa's case, confirmed to BBC Sinhala that Saudi Arabia had overturned the death sentence, adding that they are reviewing the Supreme Court's latest ruling.

Sivarasa's family had earlier said they have had no direct contact with him since 28 September.

International rights groups had also joined calls for Saudi to spare his life.

"Saudi authorities should end their use of abusive laws to hand out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offenses, especially against migrant workers who are already in a vulnerable position with limited protections," Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch, said on Tuesday.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant positive legal development where Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court overturned a death sentence related to blasphemy charges against a migrant worker. This decision reflects progress in human rights protections, particularly for vulnerable migrant workers, and has broad significance given the international diplomatic efforts and human rights implications.

articles.title: Diversify Nobel-prize nominations before it’s too late
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03220-xInternational scientific organizations are ready to help the committees that award the prizes to invite a wider range of nominators.
articles.content:
Nobel prizes need to reflect the diversity of today’s science communities, but change will take time.Credit: Niels Poulsen DK/Alamy

The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African lawyer and legal pioneer Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay on 9 October for “exceptional courage and integrity” in strengthening the institutions of international law. The previous day, the Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to Canadian writer Anne Carson for creating “new forms for contemporary literature”. That day, the Nobel-prize homepage declared that over the course of the literature prize’s history, there had been 119 recipients, 19 of them women.

More than 30% of this century’s science Nobel prizewinners immigrated: see their journeys

By contrast, the homepage made no prominent mention of the female laureates in chemistry, economics, physics or physiology or medicine when those awards were announced. All of the 2026 prizewinners in these categories are men. The closest women have come to the science prizes this year was in the announcement of the physics and chemistry Nobels by Ellen Moons, the secretary-general of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences — a detail described by one attendee of the physics announcement as “historic”.

The absence of women from the economics and science categories this year echoes previous clean sweeps for men, most recently in 2021 and 2024. However, the members of the committees that award the prizes care deeply about the imbalance, one of their representatives told Nature, and are determined to see change.

Between 2019 and 2026, science Nobels were awarded to seven women, and there were four years in which no prizewinners were women (see ‘Nobel imbalance’). During the previous two sets of eight years (2011–2018 and 2003–2010), there were five years in which only men won prizes. In 2011–2018, the winners included four women; in the preceding period, it was five.

Source: The Nobel Foundation

Back in 2018, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which awards the chemistry and physics prizes, wrote to those eligible for making prize nominations, encouraging them to put forward a more diverse range of nominees. That included asking more women to propose candidates and asking nominators to consider diversity in gender, geography and topic. The rules were also changed to allow people to nominate more than one discovery.

One barrier to more rapid change could be the nominations process itself. According to the statutes of the awarding bodies — the academy of sciences, which awards the chemistry and physics prizes, and the Karolinska Institute, which awards the prize for physiology or medicine, both in Stockholm — only a relatively small number of individuals can directly nominate candidates. These include previous Nobel laureates; professors in relevant subjects at universities in Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Iceland and Norway; members of the academy; and members of the relevant Nobel committees.

Boosting inclusivity in the Nobels

Other senior scientists can make nominations indirectly, but only if their institution first receives an official letter of invitation from one of the prize-awarding bodies. After the 2018 move to increase the diversity of nominations, letters were sent to more universities around the world. Women now comprise some 40% of this group of nominators, which bodes well for the future.

And there are other ways in which change could be expedited. In an Editorial two years ago, Nature urged the Nobel-prize-awarding bodies to seek help from some of the world’s recognized networks of universities and scientific organizations (Nature 634, 266; 2024). This could enable more letters to be sent to a wider swathe of universities globally. Those bodies said at the time that they would be willing to work with the Nobel organizations to find ways to expand the diversity of nominations. There’s also much that could be learnt from the organizers of newer prizes, especially those designed to recognize achievement among female scientists and researchers from other under-represented communities.

Increasing diversity is not the only reason for the Nobel organizations to accept offers of help. Although the prizes are among the world’s pre-eminent awards, their awarding bodies are coming under increasing pressure, and experiencing attempts at interference, from governments. If there was ever a time to build or strengthen global alliances, it is now.

One of the editors who worked on Nature’s Nobel-prize coverage noted in the 8 October Nature Briefing that calls have been made for prizes to recognize the contributions of machines to discoveries. Before that happens, prizes need to better reflect the diversity of research communities as they exist today. This matters not only for those individuals deserving of recognition, but also for the integrity of science as a whole.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights efforts to diversify Nobel Prize nominations, aiming to increase gender and geographic inclusivity in prestigious scientific awards. This represents a significant positive step toward equality and fairness in global recognition of scientific achievements, with broad societal impact and detailed context on the nomination process and ongoing changes.
articles.personality_title: Nobel committees work to include more diverse voices in prize nominations
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Nobel Prizes are very famous awards given every year to people who have made important discoveries or contributions in science, literature, and peace. But for a long time, most winners, especially in science and economics, have been men, and many come from only a few countries.

**What happened** – Recently, the groups that choose Nobel Prize winners started encouraging more people from different backgrounds to suggest nominees. They have sent letters to more universities worldwide and asked for nominations from more women and from different countries. This change began around 2018 and is slowly bringing more variety to the pool of candidates.

**Impact** – This effort matters because it helps make sure that the Nobel Prizes better reflect the wide range of people working in science and other fields today. For example, women now make up about 40% of those who can nominate candidates. This could lead to more fair recognition of important work done by women and people from different parts of the world.

**What's next step** – The Nobel organizations plan to work with global scientific groups to send even more invitations for nominations. They may also learn from newer awards that focus on recognizing women and under-represented groups. This approach could speed up change and protect the prize selection process from outside pressures.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Nobel Prize committees are actively expanding who can nominate candidates to make the awards more inclusive and representative of today’s diverse scientific community.

Esto podría llevar a un reconocimiento más justo de los trabajos importantes hechos por mujeres y personas de diferentes partes del mundo.

**Próximo paso** – Las organizaciones Nobel planean trabajar con grupos científicos globales para enviar aún más invitaciones para nominaciones. También podrían aprender de premios más nuevos que reconocen a mujeres y grupos poco representados. Esto podría acelerar el cambio y proteger el proceso de selección de presiones externas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Los comités Nobel están ampliando activamente quiénes pueden nominar candidatos para hacer los premios más inclusivos y representativos de la diversa comunidad científica actual.

articles.title: ‘Need for UN has never been greater,’ UN chief says, proposing slimmer $3.3 billion budget for 2027
articles.summary: Amid climate disruption, an AI revolution, war and growing hunger, “the need for the United Nations has never been greater,” Secretary-General António Guterres said on Tuesday, presenting a $3.3 billion programme budget proposal for next year – a cut of $40.8 million.
articles.content:
Key points

The proposed 2027 programme budget is 1.2 per cent below the 2026 approved level

UN80 Initiative reforms will continue, with more cuts, staff relocations and the abolition or downgrading of some posts

Predictable cashflow and timely payment of dues are essential as efficiency gains will not be sufficient to resolve the liquidity crisis

Divisions deepening

“The challenges before us are profound,” Mr. Guterres told the General Assembly’s Fifth Committee, comprising all 193 UN Member States that handle administrative and budgetary matters at UN Headquarters in New York.

“Geopolitical divisions continue to deepen, conflicts persist across regions and humanitarian needs are soaring, international law is trampled, climate disruption is hitting every continent and artificial intelligence is reshaping economies and societies,” said the Secretary-General.

Moreover, the planet’s collective Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), aimed at leaving no one behind, “are slipping further from reach”, Mr. Guterres said.

“And yet, in this era of uncertainty and fragmentation, the need for the United Nations has never been greater,” he declared.

Read the full statement here.

UN80 reforms: From proposal to practice

Reminding the committee that more than a year has passed since the UN80 Initiative was launched, the UN chief said “with your support, we set in motion far-reaching changes guided by a clear objective: to make the Secretariat more efficient, more effective, and better equipped to serve in a rapidly changing world.”

Taking stock of UN80 achievements, he said the Secretariat had already “moved from proposals to implementation”:

The number of underrepresented Member States fell from 28 to 26 between August 2024 and August 2026

Gender parity has been reached among internationally recruited staff

Payroll operations have been consolidated

Phase one of common administrative platforms had launched in New York and Bangkok

Some functions have moved to lower-cost duty stations

The UN Secretariat has absorbed a reduction of 3,116 regular budget posts

Through a voluntary early separation programme and reassignments, he said the impact on staff was “much smaller than what could be imagined” because planning began a year and a half in advance in the anticipated shortfalls.

Watch the Secretary-General’s introduction of the proposed 2027 budget:

Next phase

For 2027, the Secretary-General proposed additional post relocations across 12 entities, with the largest going to the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.

He also proposed abolishing some high-level posts, downgrading 14 senior positions and extending administrative platforms to Geneva, Nairobi, Vienna and Addis Ababa.

At the same time, he pointed out that the proposed budget incorporates standard-cost adjustments from the outset for the first time, so there will be no separate recosting later in the year.

Liquidity warning

However, the Secretary-General stressed that “efficiency alone cannot compensate for an unstable financial foundation”.

“Member States must fulfil their financial obligations in full and on time, as required by the UN Charter,” he said.

The Secretary-General also stressed that the world body needs predictable financing and timely payments of national dues to implement the mandates the Member States themselves have approved.

“Taken together, these measures will help address the liquidity challenges of the Organization and support the effective implementation of mandates,” he said.

Read the proposed plan and budget proposal here.

articles.personality_title: UN chief proposes leaner $3.3 billion budget to strengthen global efforts in 2027

**What happened** – On Tuesday, UN Secretary-General António Guterres presented a proposed budget of $3.3 billion for 2027, which is slightly lower than the current year’s budget. This budget aims to make the UN more efficient by continuing reforms from the UN80 Initiative. These reforms include moving staff to different locations, cutting some jobs, and improving administrative systems.

**Impact** – This proposal shows the UN’s effort to do more with less money while still tackling big problems around the world. For example, the UN has reached gender balance among its international staff and has reduced some job posts without causing major disruptions. Moving jobs to cities like Nairobi helps cut costs and spreads UN work more evenly across the globe.

He also reminded member countries that paying their dues on time is crucial for the UN to work smoothly. The budget and reforms will now be discussed and approved by the UN member states.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN is proposing a smaller, smarter budget for 2027 that supports important reforms to better handle global challenges while encouraging member countries to pay their fair share on time.

articles.personality_title_es: Jefe de la ONU propone un presupuesto más ajustado de 3.3 mil millones de dólares para fortalecer esfuerzos globales en 2027
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las Naciones Unidas enfrentan hoy muchos desafíos globales, como el cambio climático, guerras, hambre y cambios rápidos causados por tecnologías nuevas como la inteligencia artificial (IA). Estos problemas hacen que el trabajo de la ONU sea más importante que nunca.

**Qué pasó** – El martes, el Secretario General de la ONU, António Guterres, presentó un presupuesto propuesto de 3.3 mil millones de dólares para 2027, que es un poco menor al presupuesto actual. Este presupuesto busca hacer que la ONU sea más eficiente continuando con las reformas de la Iniciativa ONU80. Estas reformas incluyen mover al personal a diferentes lugares, eliminar algunos empleos y mejorar los sistemas administrativos.

**Impacto** – Esta propuesta muestra el esfuerzo de la ONU para hacer más con menos dinero mientras enfrenta grandes problemas en el mundo. Por ejemplo, la ONU ha logrado la igualdad de género entre su personal internacional y ha reducido algunos puestos sin causar grandes problemas. Mover empleos a ciudades como Nairobi ayuda a reducir costos y a distribuir el trabajo de la ONU de manera más equitativa.

**Próximo paso** – El Secretario General planea mover más personal a diferentes oficinas y mejorar las herramientas administrativas en lugares como Ginebra y Adís Abeba. También recordó a los países miembros que pagar sus cuotas a tiempo es crucial para que la ONU funcione bien. El presupuesto y las reformas ahora serán discutidos y aprobados por los estados miembros.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La ONU propone un presupuesto más pequeño y más inteligente para 2027 que apoya reformas importantes para manejar mejor los desafíos globales y anima a los países miembros a pagar su parte a tiempo.
